recentItems.title: Rare Steve Wozniak at AppleFest 1988 Boston, Apple II Computer History, Micoprocessors, Cupertino
recentItems.description:
A rare video excerpt from 1988 captures Steve Wozniak’s Keynote talk at the 1988 AppleFest event  held May 20–22, 1988, at Boston’s Hynes Convention Center.  This was a major showcase for the Apple II and Apple IIGS.   Apple Inc. was increasingly focused on the Macintosh, while still supporting its large Apple II user base. John Sculley had been CEO for five years; Steve Jobs had left Apple nearly three years earlier and was running NeXT. Steve Wozniak had stepped away from Apple’s daily operations but remained closely associated with the company as an influential voice and beloved figure among Apple II users.   This rescued VHS excerpt originally by Apple Connect gives a great look back at Steve’s appearance at this special Apple event.

Historical Context & Significance
Origins: The original 1981 AppleFest in Boston was created by 18-year-old Jonathan Rotenberg and the Boston Computer Society (BCS) as the first trade show dedicated entirely to a single microcomputer. The event's massive popularity proved the viability of single-brand computer expos, directly laying the operational groundwork for the Macworld Expo run by IDG. 
The Apple II vs. Mac Divide: By 1988, tension was high among attendees. Apple II loyalists and educators felt increasingly side-lined by corporate management, which favored the Macintosh II and System 6 developments. AppleFest served as one of the last major dedicated national gathering points where Apple II hardware, third-party developers, and user groups remained the focal point.

Overview: A concise historical summary from the Computer History Museum, detailing how Wozniak designed the Apple II in 1977. It highlights his engineering contributions and the machine's role in launching the personal computer industry.

3. Apple II History: The Apple Story (BYTE Magazine Interview)

Overview: A digitized two-part interview originally published in a 1984 issue of BYTE Magazine. In it, Wozniak discusses the deep technical details of creating the Apple II, including how he designed the revolutionary floppy disk controller.

Overview: A modern retrospective interview published in 2022. Wozniak reflects on the design choices he made 45 years prior, his implementation of low-cost color graphics, and the machine's radically open nature.

recentItems.title: Computer History IBM OS/2 Warp Original Promo film 1994 Nimoy, Kate Mulgrew Star Trek Voyager Win 95
recentItems.description:
Computer History: Rare IBM “OS/2 Warp” Original IBM Promotional Presentation, 1994, excerpt.  (No AI)    In 1994, IBM released OS/2 operating system version 3.0, branding it “OS/2 Warp” to leverage Star Trek’s iconic themes of speed and power.
To help promote the launch of Warp, IBM hired Leonard Nimoy (“Mr. Spock”) and Kate Mulgrew, the newly cast Captain Janeway of Star Trek: Voyager.  Speaking separately, they starred in an hour-long, live satellite presentation broadcast on October 11, 1994.  This excerpt contains the talks of Leonard Nimoy and Kate Mulgrew and runs about 12 minutes.  During this time period, Microsoft was continuing to test its upcoming Windows 95 operating system, and was many months behind its planned release date of late 1994.  (It was finally released in August 1995.)   IBM took advantage of this delay by Microsoft and claimed it was time now, to embrace IBM’s new OS/2 Warp operating system.  The hour long presentation was a major televised media event for IBM.  --  Kate Mulgrew's talk begins 
around 07:12

Also, Patrick Steward (Star Trek’s Captain Picard) was scheduled to speak as master of ceremonies, but conflicts with Paramount’s copyrights related to Star Trek terminology and actors.  Kate Mulgrew was enlisted to fill this role in a nearly last minute change.
* * This appearance of Kate Mulgrew discussing her role as Captain Janeway was months before her appearance in “Star Trek: Voyager” series which first aired in January 1995.
Provided for historical preservation, educational interest and comment.
Please let us know if you have experiences with IBM OS/2 Warp that you’d like to share by leaving your thoughts in the comments section.
Thank you!

Computer History Archives Project (CHAP)

recentItems.title: Computer History: Secret Origin of Remington 409 & UNIVAC 60 Vacuum Tube Cage Plugboard Programming
recentItems.description:
Computer History: The secret origin of the Remington Rand 409 computer and Tube and Cage technology of UNIVAC 60 -120.  In 1943, under absolute secrecy, Remington Rand initiated development of a revolutionary commercial computing machine in Rowayton, Connecticut.
Under the direction of  former Manhattan Project director General Leslie Groves, two independent engineering teams Constructed the prototype  Remington Rand 409, between 1949 and 1951.  The 409 represented a key evolutionary link bridging mechanical punched card tabulators and stored-program electronic computers.  

The Remington 409 utilized 1,000 vacuum tubes and was the first computer used by the IRS (1952) and the foundation of the UNIVAC 60 tube and cage computer line.  Video shows origin of the 409, behind the scenes of creating the tube-cage and plugboard design with video images of the early vacuum tube modules.  Describes the use of the TELEPHONE DIAL on the RR 409 and UNIVAC 60 machines, and plugboard programming processes.

The release years for these Remington Rand card-programmed computing systems (originally developed as part of the Remington Rand 409 series) are:
Remington Rand 409 prototype DEMO – 1951
Remington Rand 409 delivery to IRS – 1951
UNIVAC model 60 released – 1952
UNIVAC model 120 released – 1953
UNIVAC model 40 released – 1955

Runtime 8 minutes

Uploaded by Computer History Archives Project (CHAP) for educational and historical purposes.  (Disclaimer:  Some AI enhancement of the AUDIO.    All video is original. No AI video.)

recentItems.title: Remembering DEC "Components Group" Digital Equipment 1978 Mini Computers PDP promo Marlborough Mass.
recentItems.description:
Vintage Computers:  A Rare 1970s Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) promo film about the "Components Group," established June 1974.  This fascinating promo explains the the purpose of the "Components Group" and shows the manufacturing facilities and employees of the time period.  Housed in the former RCA computer facility at Marlborough, Mass. Full color, runs 2mins.   Uploaded by Computer History Archives Project (CHAP)

SEE ALSO:  PICTORIAL HISTORY OF DEC:  (Courtesy of the Computer History Museum)
featuring many models of the DEC PDP and VAX machines and more.
https://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2018/08/102740410-05-01-acc.pdf

A BIT OF HISTORY OF THE MARLBOROUGH, Mass. FACILITY
In January 1974, DEC purchased RCA's huge Marlborough facility, which had been largely unused since RCA’s exit from the commercial computing business in 1971.  This impressively modern 700,000 sq. ft. facility had been designed by modernist architect Vincent Kling.   It now provided valuable expansion room for DEC, originally housing its “DECsystem-10 group.” 

In June 1974, DEC established its Components Group and stationed them inside the landmark Marlborough Tower. This group was formed to sell independent, "unbundled" peripherals, like terminal keyboards and tape drives and the PDP-8A computer, directly to large-volume customers and OEMs.

Years later, the Marlborough building also played a vital role in preserving computer history. In 1979, DEC vice president Gordon Bell and his wife, Gwen Bell, used the open-balcony lobby of the Tower Building to launch the Digital Computer Museum. 

This collection eventually spun out as an independent entity and became the famous Boston Computer Museum, and ultimately formed the core collection of today's Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California.

Film rescued and provided by
Periscope Film

DEC’s products, employees, and operations were then absorbed into Compaq. Compaq itself was acquired by Hewlett-Packard in 2002.

recentItems.title: Do you remember IBM SYSTEM/390 MAINFRAME COMPUTER with MVS/ESA? Security Software Multimedia
recentItems.description:
1992 IBM SYSTEM/390 MAINFRAME COMPUTER Security Multimedia Software Hardware:  In this 1992 episode of IBM System/390 Magazine the focus is on IBM mainframe technology during one of the most important eras in enterprise computing.
The early 1990s were a critical period for IBM’s large-scale systems. The System/390 platform, running MVS/ESA, supported the demanding workloads of banks, insurance companies, government agencies, manufacturers, universities, and other major organizations. These systems handled security, transaction processing, databases, software development, networking, and large-scale business operations long before modern cloud computing became common.   * MVS/ESA (Multiple Virtual Storage/Enterprise Systems Architecture)

This video is a partially restored excerpt from a damaged 34 year old VHS tape.  This segment  highlights key mainframe topics of the time, including security, software, hardware, multimedia, and enterprise computing strategy. It also shows how IBM positioned the System/390 as a powerful, reliable, and scalable platform for mission-critical business environments.

Computer History Archives Project (CHAP) documents and preserves vintage computing history through original hardware, publications, photographs, and historical research.  preserve the history of IBM mainframe computing and remind us how central mainframes were to the information systems that supported business, government, and industry throughout the 1990s.  Full color, runs 24 mins.    Narrators are Tom Ellis and Roxanne Stein

Your comments and experiences with the IBM Mainframe environment from this era or any other era are warmly invited.   See also our other videos and playlists.

recentItems.title: What happened to NYNEX Cell Phones??  1995 (ATT Telecom Verizon Motorola)
recentItems.description:
What Happened to NYNEX Cell Phones?   1995 Mobile Phone Technology, "BEHIND THE SCENES."  Part of Bell Atlantic, ATT, Verizon History.  Fascinating look back at this groundbreaking technology over a decade before the first Apple iPhone!  Do you remember using NYNEX?    New York, New England eXchange cellular telephone network.   Partially restored training video.   Enjoy this look back into the past.  Share your favorite NYNEX or Motorola Cell Phone stories?   ~    

Uploaded by Computer History Archives Project (CHAP)

NYNEX Corporation was one of the original Regional Bell Operating Companies (RBOCs)—commonly known as "Baby Bells"—created following the antitrust breakup of AT&T. It was formed on January 1, 1984, and served the northeastern United States.
The name NYNEX is an acronym derived from New York and New England eXchange.

Core Operations & Territory

NYNEX primary provided regulated wire telephone services through its two main operating subsidiaries:
• New York Telephone: Serving New York State and a small portion of northern New Jersey.
• New England Telephone: Serving Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Vermont.

Cellular Pioneering
Beyond traditional landlines, NYNEX was a major pioneer in the early wireless industry through NYNEX Mobile Communications.
• In 1995, NYNEX merged its cellular operations with Bell Atlantic Mobile to create a massive joint venture wireless network.
• This joint entity ultimately laid the structural groundwork for what became Verizon Wireless.
• Motorola was NYNEX Mobile’s leading supplier for customer phones.  NYNEX Mobile’s overall cellular support included AT&T, Qualcomm, Northern Telecom/Nortel, and others.
The Motorola MicroTAC was a groundbreaking family of semi-clamshell and flip mobile phones first released by Motorola in 1989. It revolutionized the mobile industry by introducing a folding mouthpiece to drastically reduce the phone's bulk.

recentItems.title: What happened to TOSHIBA SATELLITE Laptops? video training 1994; A world leader in Laptop computers
recentItems.description:
Computer History Laptops, Notebooks: Toshiba manufactured laptop computers for 35 years, from 1985 to 2020.  During their peak year 2011, they sold 17.7 million alone. Toshiba was in the top 5 laptop computer makers in the world.   This restored 10 minute segment from an early Toshiba Satellite training video shows the specifics of the Satellite Notebook computer in nice detail.  Remember the PS/2 compatible ports and the PCMCIA cards, and side roller ball?  Hope you enjoy this look back at some 1990’s laptop tech.  

What Happened to Toshiba Laptops?
By 2017, competition from Lenovo, HP, Dell and others caused a rapid drop in sales.  Toshiba decided to sell its PC division to Sharp Corporation.  Sharp partially resurrected the “Satellite” name in 2020, calling their computer the “Dynabook Satellite Pro.”

Detailed Info:
Originally, Toshiba’s laptop business began with the Toshiba T1100 in 1985, often described by Dynabook as the first mass-market laptop. During the 1990s and 2000s, Toshiba became a major notebook brand, with Satellite and Satellite Pro serving the consumer and small-business/professional markets. The Satellite Pro name was later discontinued under Toshiba as the company reduced its PC presence, but the product identity did not vanish.

In April 2016, Toshiba’s PC-related businesses were transferred into Toshiba Client Solutions Co., Ltd. In October 2018, Toshiba sold 80.1% of that company to Sharp Corporation. In January 2019, Toshiba Client Solutions was renamed Dynabook Inc. Finally, in August 2020, Toshiba transferred its remaining 19.9% stake to Sharp, making Dynabook a wholly owned Sharp subsidiary. Today, Satellite Pro continues as a Dynabook business laptop line, including current C-series models such as the Satellite Pro C50.
see also:
https://dynabook.com/global/en/index.html

also, its key to remember that 
Alan Kay, American computer scientist who pioneered work on object-oriented programming and windowing graphical user interface design, conceived the Dynabook ides around 1968 and described it in his 1972 paper “A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages.”   Long before Sharp used the name, Kay's idea was a portable, notebook-sized personal computer with a screen, keyboard/tablet-style interaction, graphical interface, networking, and educational software — essentially a vision of the laptop/tablet decades before the hardware was practical. The Computer History Museum describes Kay’s 1968 Dynabook mockup as too advanced to build at the time, but highly influential.

recentItems.title: Rare 1941 film: Pre-Computer Calculating Accounting Machines & IBM 416 punch card tabulators WW2 405
recentItems.description:
A partially restored original film showing electrical calculating, bookkeeping, accounting machines in operation. Burroughs Electric Duplex, Monroe, Friden Rotary Calculator, Underwood Elliott Fisher, and Comptometer brands all battled for market share with increasing capabilities of their machines. 
Includes very rare footage of the IBM 416 Punched Card Accounting Machine (08:52), of 1941,
originally made in Italy.  Produced only in limited numbers, the only known remaining machine today is in the IBM Hursley Museum (Hampshire, UK), a secure IBM research facility not open to the public.  The museum obtained their 416 machine from IBM Oslo, Norway around 2017, and it is now part of the Hursley’s wartime computing machines exhibit not open to the public.   The 416 is a numerical only machine (no text), and a variant of the IBM 405 machines produced in larger quantities.

Overall this film is a  fascinating look at a select group of vintage office machines of the 1940's era, and the IBM 416 specifically. This film runs 10 minutes, with sound and original narration. 

With thanks to Periscope Film for rescuing this film, and providing it to CHAP under license.  Periscope Film is a leading stock footage provider

recentItems.title: UNIVAC FACTORY TOUR 1968 Mainframe Film Restored "Electronic Servants" Twin Cities Minnesota (No AI)
recentItems.description:
Computer History: UNIVAC FACTORY TOUR.  "Electronic Servants" (1968) a  behind-the-scenes look at the high-precision manufacturing and assembly processes at the UNIVAC "Twin Cities" facilities in Minnesota during the peak of the mainframe era.  This full color film was shot largely at the Roseville facility, Sperry Univac’s Commercial Computer facility at that time.  It highlights skilled workers involved in the creation of the massive UNIVAC 1108 and UNIVAC 494 and 418 systems.    This original film served as both a public relations piece and a detailed technical overview of how the massive computer systems were built.  Original narration shows numerous technically skilled employees at work, clean room operations, component manufacturing of both discrete components to integrated circuits, core memory assembly including threading tiny ferrite cores onto copper wires by hand and machine, printed circuit boards, the Uniscope video terminal,  large magnetic drum storage units and more.  Includes a high-resolution digital image gallery after the film.  Total run time about 23 mins.  (Some original background music was removed for copyright reasons, but ALL video is intact, no AI image content, all original color.)     A vintage UNIVAC Computer History Film. Uploaded by the Computer History Archives Project (CHAP) for educational review and comment.

recentItems.title: Rare Control Data FILM: CDC 6600 Super Computer CERN Labs Switzerland Seymour Cray 1965 Electronics
recentItems.description: Computer History:  CDC 6600 SuperComputer, by Semour Cray.   The CONTROL DATA CORPORATION 6600 use at CERN Laboratories, Geneva, Switzerland.  Original footage!   The CDC 6600 computer was designed by Seymour Cray.  (Film of the CDC 6600 starts 03:13. )   CERN is also famous for its use of large-scale and supercomputing technology from the 1960's up to today.  From 1958 to 1993, over 18 different computer systems were utilized by CERN in its research projects.  CERN took delivery of its CDC 6600 Supercomputer in September 1965.   Video shows the CDC 6600 computer in action at CERN's laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland along with the particle accelerator "Proton Synchrotron".     CERN roughly translates to:  “European Organization for Nuclear Research.” Their modern research into advanced particle physics is known world-wide.  {Note:  Original CERN and CDC film content from 1960s, plus some AI assisted narration for improved audio.}   Film runs about 5 mins.
